title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet III: preparations for the journey
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), SB III) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet III: 164 of 209 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (8 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
The elders advise Gilgamesh. His mother, the goddess Ninsun, prays to Shamash for his protection and adopts Enkidu. The two heroes leave Uruk for the Forest of Cedar.

The Standard Babylonian version of the epic, traditionally ascribed to the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni, was written on twelve tablets. Most surviving copies come from the libraries of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE) and from Babylon and other Babylonian cities (7th-2nd century BCE). This page gives Tablet III in the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition by A. R. George (2022 and later revisions).

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/III) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 164 of the 209 lines of the eBL edition (78%), from 8 tablets in the British Museum: BM.98990 (Nineveh), K.4474 (Nineveh), K.3423 (Nineveh), K.9885 (Nineveh), K.8558 (Nineveh), BM.35079, BM.32960, BM.36093.

Lines not shown. 45 of the 209 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 23 (no photograph in eBL: BM.34191); 29-30 (no photograph in eBL: BM.34191); 59 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76873 (Iraq Museum)); 85 (no photograph in eBL: VAT.19286 (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin), IM.76873 (Iraq Museum)); 109-116 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76873 (Iraq Museum)); 122a (no photograph in eBL: IM.76873 (Iraq Museum)); 133-136 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76873 (Iraq Museum)); 164-165 (no photograph in eBL: K.8573); 166-173 (no photograph in eBL: K.8573, BM.34191); 207-222 (no photograph in eBL: BM.34191); 244 (no manuscript preserves it). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; / alternative readings; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet.

translation.text:
1‘[Come back in safety] to [the quay of] Uruk!
2Do not trust, O Gilgameš, in the fullness of your strength,
3let your eyes be satisfied, strike a blow to rely on!
4“He who goes in front saves (his) comrade,
5he who knew the road protected his friend.”
6Let Enkidu go in front of you,
7he knows the way to the Forest of Cedar!
8He is tried in battles and experienced in combat,
9let Enkidu protect (his) friend and keep safe (his) comrade!
10let him bring his person back to his wives!
11In this our assembly we hereby give the king into your care:
12you will ensure (his) return and give the king into our care.’
13Gilgameš opened his mouth to speak,
14saying to Enkidu:
15‘Come, my friend, let us go to Egal-maḫ,
16into the presence of the great Queen Ninsun!
17Ninsun is clever, she is wise, she knows everything,
18she will set steps of (good) counsel for our feet.’
19They took each other hand in hand,
20Gilgameš and Enkidu, as they went to Egal-maḫ.
21Into the presence of the great Queen Ninsun,
22Gilgameš arose and entered before [the goddess, his mother.]
24‘O Ninsun, I have grown so bold [as to travel]
25the distant path to where Ḫumbaba is.
26I shall face a battle that I do not know,
27I shall ride a road that I do not know.
28I hereby beseech you, give me your blessing, so that I may go,
translation.scan_note: British Museum BM.98990: obverse, column i, the tablet's own lines 1 to 27. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/III) attributes SB III 1-28 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges (ink number 98990, registration 1904-10-9,13); a full column on the obverse and a few lines on the reverse, consistent with eBL's columns i (27 lines) and vi (11 lines). On this tablet of lines 1, 27-28 only one to three signs survive and lines 2-6, 8-9, 11, 20-22, 24-26 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. Lines 7, 10, 12-19 are complete on this tablet. eBL line(s) 23 fall within this run but are not on this tablet (they are listed among the lines not shown).

96Your fleet-footed mules shall bring you (in) early,
97let a restful seat, a bed … (scribal annotation: broken) be laid out for you
97aa seat of […]
98The gods, your brothers, shall bring food [to delight] you,
99may Aya the Bride wipe your face with her clean garment-fringe!’
100Again Wild-Cow Ninsun repeated (her) behest before Šamaš:
101‘O Šamaš, will not Gilgameš rank with the gods?
102Will he not share the heavens with you?
103Will he not share a sceptre with the moon?
104Will he not become wise with Ea of the Apsû?
105Will he not rule the black-headed race with Irnina?
106[Will he] not dwell in the Land-of-No-Return with Ningišzida?
107Let me make him, O Šamaš, […] …
108may he not … may he not […] the [Forest] of [Cedar.]

translation.text:
117[Wild-Cow] Ninsun was clever, [she was wise, she knew everything,]
118[…] Gilgameš … […]
119she smothered the censer and came [down from the roof]
120She summoned Enkidu to declare (her) intention:
121‘O mighty Enkidu, you are not the offspring of my womb,
122but now your brood (will be) with the oblates of Gilgameš,
123the priestesses, hierodules and temple girls.’
124She placed the symbols on Enkidu’s neck:
125‘The priestesses took in the foundling,
126and the Divine Daughters will bring up the foster-child.
127I myself hereby adopt Enkidu, whom [I love], as a son,
128let Gilgameš in [brotherhood] treat Enkidu with favour!
129Now … […]
130And […] … […]
131while [you] travel [together] to the Forest of Cedar,
132let [the days be] long, let the nights be short!
